mechanical-design-engineering.applications: New product development, drawing preparation, component redesign and reverse engineering.
mechanical-design-engineering.decision: Start with the function and interfaces: what must the part do, what must it fit, and which dimensions cannot change? Include assembly access, material preferences and the intended production quantity.
mechanical-design-engineering.outputs: Agree the required CAD format, drawing revision, dimensional information and review milestones before design work begins.
questions: Can I start with a sample or a sketch?

A sketch, sample or existing drawing can be a starting point. Include the intended use, dimensions you know and the problem you want to solve. Measurement needs and the design scope are reviewed before work is agreed.
Which design files should I prepare?
List the CAD and drawing formats you have, their revision and any files needed to understand the assembly. The required exchange format and final deliverables are agreed during the technical review.

sheet-metal-fabrication.applications: Brackets, folded panels, housings, guards and multi-part sheet metal assemblies.
sheet-metal-fabrication.decision: Material grade, sheet thickness and bend geometry influence how a part is made. Identify critical holes, mating surfaces, visible faces and any welding or finishing requirements.
sheet-metal-fabrication.outputs: Agree the drawing revision, material, quantities, finish and inspection points, including which dimensions apply before or after finishing.
questions: What information helps with a sheet metal enquiry?

Share a dimensioned drawing or CAD model, material grade, thickness and quantity. Mark critical fits and identify the required finish. If a flat pattern is available, include it with the formed-part drawing.
Should the surface finish be decided before fabrication?
Include it in the initial brief. Coating, masking, visible surfaces and assembly fits can affect hole sizes, joining and the sequence of operations.

precision-machining.applications: Shafts, spacers, brackets, housings and components with defined mating features.
precision-machining.decision: Separate critical fits from general dimensions. Material grade, tolerance, surface finish and batch quantity affect the machining and inspection approach.
precision-machining.outputs: Agree the current drawing, material specification, critical dimensions, inspection requirements and any documentation needed with the parts.
questions: Do all dimensions need the tightest tolerance?
State the tolerances required for the component to function. Identify the mating parts and critical features so the machining and inspection plan can focus on the dimensions that matter.
What should I include for a repeat batch?
Provide the approved drawing revision, material, quantity and any relevant inspection records or approved sample information. Flag changes from the previous version explicitly.

product-manufacturing.applications: Prototypes, low-volume products, OEM components and complete mechanical assemblies.
product-manufacturing.decision: Define whether the next milestone is a functional prototype, design validation or a production batch. Identify unresolved design choices before estimating the production route.
product-manufacturing.outputs: Agree the product definition, bill of materials where available, approval sample requirements, quantity and acceptance criteria.
questions: Can a project begin with a prototype?

Include the purpose of the prototype and what you need to learn from it, such as fit, assembly or usability. The prototype scope and its relationship to a later production version are agreed separately.
What changes between a prototype and a batch?
Materials, tooling, assembly methods and inspection plans may need review. Confirm the approved revision and any changes before treating a prototype as a production reference.

surface-treatment-finishing.applications: Furniture frames, visible panels, enclosures and fabricated or machined metal components.
surface-treatment-finishing.decision: Choose the finish around the base material, intended environment and appearance. Specify visible faces, colour references, texture and any areas that must remain uncoated.
surface-treatment-finishing.outputs: Agree preparation, finish reference, masking, acceptance criteria and how finished parts should be handled and packed.
questions: Is a colour name enough to specify a finish?
A physical sample or an agreed colour reference is more useful. Also specify the intended texture and gloss, because surfaces with the same colour can look different under different lighting.
Which areas may need masking?
Identify threaded holes, electrical contact points, precision mating surfaces and other features that must remain free of coating. The masking requirements should be clear in the brief.

welding-fabrication.applications: Frames, supports, enclosures and custom fabricated assemblies.
welding-fabrication.decision: Share the assembly geometry, material grades and joint requirements. Identify distortion-sensitive dimensions, access restrictions and the final surface finish.
welding-fabrication.outputs: Agree assembly drawings, weld requirements, inspection criteria and any applicable project-specific procedure or documentation requirements.
questions: What should a fabrication drawing show?
Include overall dimensions, member or sheet sizes, material grades, joint details and critical interfaces. Add assembly references where the part connects to other equipment or furniture.
How should inspection requirements be specified?
State the intended application and required acceptance criteria in the brief. Any project-specific testing, procedure qualification or documentation needs must be reviewed and agreed explicitly.

quality-inspection.applications: Dimensional checks, component verification, assembly inspection and documented acceptance reviews.
quality-inspection.decision: Inspection starts with an approved reference. Identify the drawing revision, features to measure, acceptance limits and the reporting format you need.
quality-inspection.outputs: Agree measurement scope, sampling requirements, report format and how any non-conforming observations will be recorded.
questions: What is needed before a component can be inspected?
Provide the current drawing or specification and identify the dimensions or characteristics that require verification. Include reference datums, acceptance limits and the quantity of parts.
Can inspection results be documented?
State the required report format and traceability information when enquiring. The scope, measurement method and documentation to be supplied are agreed before inspection.

assembly-integration.applications: Mechanical subassemblies, complete products and assemblies combining mechanical and electrical elements.
assembly-integration.decision: A clear bill of materials and assembly sequence help identify missing parts and access issues. Include fastening, cable routing, adjustment and functional test requirements.
assembly-integration.outputs: Agree component responsibilities, assembly revision, inspection and test steps, labelling and packaging requirements.
questions: What should I prepare for an assembly enquiry?
Provide the bill of materials, assembly drawings, component supply plan and quantity. Include work instructions or a reference sample if available, plus the checks required before dispatch.
Should packaging be considered during assembly planning?
Yes. Share the delivery route, protection needs and whether the product will travel fully assembled or in sections. Packing and any installation requirements should be agreed with the scope.

project-manufacturing-solutions.applications: Projects requiring coordinated design, multiple manufacturing processes, finishing and assembly.
project-manufacturing-solutions.decision: Define the final deliverable, current project stage and approval responsibilities. Identify cost, timing or process challenges so they can be discussed in the context of the complete project.
project-manufacturing-solutions.outputs: Agree the scope, review milestones, responsibilities, documentation and acceptance process for each stage.
questions: Can one brief include several manufacturing processes?
Yes. Include the complete product or assembly requirement rather than only individual parts. This allows design, fabrication, machining, finishing and assembly dependencies to be reviewed together.
How should I describe a cost-reduction project?
Share the current design, expected quantities and the functions that must be preserved. Identify known material, assembly or process concerns and any restrictions on changing the design.
